title: How to Apply Without Getting Scammed
subtitle: Everything you just learned in this course is also a script. This module is how to keep it yours.

blocks.text: A whole course of real programs, real deadlines and real dollar amounts is exactly the raw material a scammer needs. They do not have to invent a convincing lie about veterans’ benefits or home renovation grants or GST rebates. The real programs already come with real names, real numbers and real urgency built in.
All a scam has to do is borrow the name and change who is asking for your information.

This final module is not about fraud in general. It is about the moment when everything else in this course can be used against you, and the few habits that close that door no matter which program’s name gets borrowed next: one fact, five signs, one sentence to say, and a few locks to set before anyone knocks.
One simple habit can protect every benefit in this course from people who borrow its name.
blocks.detail: Scams copy real programs, real numbers and real deadlines, so knowing the program is not enough on its own.
blocks.extra: Section 02 gives you the one fact that ends most scams.

sections.title: The One Fact That Ends Most of These Before They Start

blocks.text: No government department in Canada will call, text or email you to demand payment now, threaten arrest, or ask for bank details, a credit card number or your full Social Insurance Number over the phone. That includes the CRA, Veterans Affairs, Natural Resources Canada and Employment and Social Development Canada. Every one of these departments says so, in writing.
Legitimate government contact looks unglamorous by comparison. None of it arrives with the emotional temperature of a threat, and none of it needs an answer in the next twenty minutes.

items.title: A real program
list: A message in an online account you logged into yourself
Time to read, check and call back
Payment, if any, through your own bank or the official site
Free to learn about and free to apply for

items.title: A scam
list: A call, text or email you did not expect
Gift cards, crypto, an e-transfer to a person or a courier
A link to click instead of a login
A fee to get something that is free

items.title: “If they knew my name, my address and mentioned a real program, it must be legitimate.”
items.text: Scammers do more homework now, and fake caller ID can show a real government number. Knowing your details or a real program name shows someone did research, not who they work for. Check through a channel you control, using a number you looked up yourself.

blocks.text: CRA: Scams and fraud

sections.title: Five Signs, Whichever Program’s Name Gets Used

blocks.text: Different scripts, same structure. Recognizing the structure matters more than memorizing any single version, because the version changes every tax season and the structure does not. Here are the five signs, one at a time.

items.title: COUNTDOWN
items.text: Pay in thirty minutes or face arrest or lose the benefit. Real programs do not run on a clock that starts when you answer.

items.title: ODD PAYMENT
items.text: Gift cards, crypto, an e-transfer to a person or cash by courier. No government department takes any of these.

items.title: A LINK
items.text: A text or email pushing you to click to claim a refund. Real programs tell you to log in the way you normally do.

items.title: A FEE
items.text: Paying to hear about a grant, or a cut of an award before you apply. Every real program in this course is free.

items.title: UNASKED
items.text: A call about a grant you never applied for, a rebate you never asked for or a review you never started.

blocks.text: One sign is a reason to slow down. Two or more is a reason to stop, hang up and check through your own door.

Do not call the number the caller gave you. Do not click the link in the text or email. Instead, look up the department’s number yourself, from a letter you already have or a search you run, and contact them that way. If the contact was real, this costs a few minutes and confirms it. If it was fake, you have closed the door without giving anything up. It is the one rule worth memorizing word for word.

items.title: Real benefit offers don’t arrive with a ticking clock.
items.text: Real benefit offers don’t arrive with a ticking clock.

items.title: Look up the number yourself, and contact them that way.
items.text: Look up the number yourself, and contact them that way.

blocks.text: Saying it out loud is the hard part, so have the words ready. This works on any caller, ends any countdown and costs nothing to say:
“I need to call you back. I will use the number on my own letter.”
A real caller will say that is fine. A scammer will push harder, get angry or suddenly offer a discount. Either way, you have your answer.

sections.title: What a Real Application Actually Needs From You

blocks.text: Across this course, real programs asked for ID, income figures, medical forms and bank details for direct deposit. They always did it through a form you opened yourself, on a site you went to on your own. None of them asked for it on a phone call you did not expect.

Your Social Insurance Number needs special care. Some real applications require it. It is also one of the most valuable things a fraudster can get to build a fake identity. Give it only when you started the contact, on an official government site or form. If you are not sure a form needs it, ask the organization first, using a number you looked up yourself.

The paid “helper” showed up in the Small-Business Grants lesson, and it applies just as much to a veteran’s disability claim, a senior’s renovation grant or a training credit. Every free helper named in this course exists so nobody has to pay for this: Service Officers, Community Futures, Small Business Enterprise Centres, employment counsellors and 211.

items.title: “A grant consultant with a professional website and a logo must be legitimate.”
items.text: A website costs little to build, and a logo can be made to look close to an official one without copying it. Neither proves a link to government. The proof that matters is whether the program is on the official page, and whether you can apply to it yourself for free.

sections.title: Lock the Doors Before Anyone Knocks

blocks.text: The best time to protect your benefits is on a quiet afternoon, not in the middle of a call. These four take under an hour, together.

items.title: Your own CRA account
items.text: Register for CRA My Account and turn on email notices. You will see your real balance and messages, and hear when your address or deposit details change.

items.title: Saved real numbers
items.text: Save the CRA, Service Canada and your provincial office numbers from official letters, in your phone and on paper.

items.title: Bank alerts
items.text: Turn on alerts for every e-transfer, new payee and large withdrawal, so a problem shows up in minutes, not weeks.

items.title: A household rule
items.text: Agree with the people you live with: nobody pays or shares a number on a call they did not start.

items.title: “Scammers only go after people who are not careful.”
items.text: These scripts are tested on thousands of people and built to work on careful people in a hurry. Locks set in advance work when attention runs out.

sections.title: What to Do If You Already Gave Something Up

blocks.text: This happens to careful people. What you do next matters more than the mistake, and speed matters more than shame. If money moved, call your bank or card company right away. Some payments can still be stopped or reversed in the first few hours. If you shared your SIN, bank details or other personal information, contact the department yourself, using a number you look up, and ask about fraud alerts on your account. Report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre whether or not you lost money. Being targeted is not a judgment on you.

items.title: Call your bank or card company
items.text: Ask them to stop or reverse the payment and lock the account.

items.title: Call the real department
items.text: Use a number from an official letter. Ask them to flag your file.

items.title: Add credit fraud alerts
items.text: Ask Equifax and TransUnion to put a fraud alert on your credit file, so lenders check it is really you.

items.title: Report it
items.text: Call the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1‑888‑495‑8501, or report online. Call police if you lost money.

blocks.text: Before you respond to anything claiming to be from a government program

items.title: I did not initiate this contact, or I am not certain who initiated it.
I am being asked to act within an unusually short window.
I am being asked to pay by gift card, cryptocurrency, e-transfer to a person, or courier.
I am being asked to click a link rather than log into an account I navigate to myself.
I am being asked for my SIN, full banking details, or a credit card number before I have verified who is asking.
I have not yet looked up the department’s number independently and called it myself.

blocks.text: If more than one of these is true, stop. Hang up, close the message, and verify independently before doing anything else.
Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre

sections.title: Harold, the Courier, and the Phone Call He Made Instead

blocks.text: Harold and the call he made instead
paragraphs: Harold is sixty-eight and lives in Winnipeg. His goal this year is to stay on top of his bills on a fixed income. Then his phone rings on a Tuesday afternoon.

The man says he is with the Canada Revenue Agency. Harold owes several thousand dollars in back taxes from a benefit overpayment, he says, and a warrant will be issued within the hour unless it is paid now. The caller ID shows a number that looks official.

The man is patient, which in hindsight is its own kind of pressure. He stays on the line. He explains exactly what to say to a courier who will come to collect the cash. He keeps saying this is routine and that he is helping Harold avoid something much worse. Harold is not usually anxious about much, but his hands are shaking.

Then Harold remembers one sentence. Months earlier, after a news story about this exact scam, his daughter told him: if anyone calls saying they are the CRA and you owe money, hang up and call the real number yourself.
Harold makes his choice. He tells the man he needs to call him back. He hangs up. Then he dials the number on last year’s Notice of Assessment, not the number the caller gave him.

The real CRA has no record of any debt, any warrant or any call. That afternoon, Harold reports it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. The next weekend, he tells his neighbour the same sentence his daughter told him.
Nothing is lost except twenty minutes and one unpleasant hour.

items.title: TUESDAY CALL
items.text: A warrant “within the hour”

items.title: ONE SENTENCE
items.text: Hang up, call the real number

items.title: THAT AFTERNOON
items.text: Reported to the CAFC

blocks.text: Harold kept his savings by hanging up and calling the real CRA number himself.
blocks.detail: The same one sentence can protect you, and anyone you pass it on to.
blocks.extra: Your action this week, in Section 10, starts with saving the real numbers.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: A caller says the CRA will issue a warrant in an hour unless you pay. What do you do?
items.detail: Hang up. Call the CRA yourself on a number from your own letter or the official site. The CRA does not threaten arrest by phone.

items.title: A text says your GST rebate is ready and gives a link. What do you do?
items.detail: Do not click. Log into CRA My Account the way you normally do and check there.

items.title: Someone asks for a fee to help you apply for a free government grant. Which sign is that?
items.detail: Number 4, a fee to get something free. Every real program in this course is free to apply for.

items.title: You paid a scammer by e-transfer ten minutes ago. What comes first?
items.detail: Call your bank right away. Some payments can still be stopped in the first few hours.

items.title: What sentence ends any suspicious call?
items.detail: “I need to call you back.” Then use a number you looked up yourself.

items.title: Why report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre if you lost nothing?
items.detail: Reports help track patterns and stop the next scam. Small reports add up.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Verification Habit

blocks.text: This week: save the real phone numbers for the CRA, Service Canada and your provincial benefits office where you will find them under pressure. Tell one person in your life the single rule from this module: verify through a number you looked up yourself, never the one you were given. If anything in the past year felt off, report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre now. It is never too late to matter.
Verify through a door you opened yourself.
blocks.detail: No government department demands payment now by phone, text or email, or accepts gift cards, crypto or cash by courier. Check any contact you did not expect through a number you look up yourself, set your locks on a quiet day, and if something gets through, report it and move fast.

items.title: Spoofed caller ID
items.text: A trick that shows a fake number on your phone, including real government numbers.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: An email or text made to look official, meant to get you to click a link or share information.

items.title: CAFC
items.text: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. The national body that collects fraud reports across Canada. The RCMP, the Ontario Provincial Police and the Competition Bureau run it together.

items.title: Verification through an independent channel
items.text: Contacting an organization with a number or address you found yourself, not one given by the person contacting you.

items.title: Fraud alert
items.text: A note on your credit file that asks lenders to confirm it is really you before opening new credit.

items.title: Smishing
items.text: A scam sent by text message, usually with a link.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: 1-888-495-8501, or report online at antifraudcentre.ca. Report every incident, even if nothing was lost.
Canada Revenue Agency: 1-800-959-8281 for individuals, to confirm whether a contact claiming to be the CRA is genuine.
Your bank or card issuer: immediately, if money has moved or account details were shared.
Local police, non-emergency line: if you have lost money or believe your identity has been compromised.

blocks.text: If you are in immediate danger or a crime is in progress, call 911.
